1331.title: Honest placebo
1331.hook: pills openly labeled as placebo still helped some patients (Kaptchuk et al., 2010)
1331.howItsDone: Researchers study "open-label" placebos by telling patients plainly that the pills contain no medicine; people, religious or not, also keep small daily rituals, such as lighting a candle or making tea, to mark a beginning.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was when to see someone: practice is good company, not a doctor. Your line was care first.

A patient sits across from a clinician and is handed a bottle of pills. The clinician explains, plainly, that there's no medicine in them. They're placebo pills, inert, like sugar pills. Take them twice a day anyway. No trick, nothing hidden. It sounds like the setup for a joke. It was a real study. And the patients who took the honest placebo reported feeling better than the patients who got no pills at all. So what on earth was in that bottle?
screen: `NO MEDICINE IN THESE.` → `TAKE THEM ANYWAY.` → `THEY FELT BETTER.`

segments.voice: First, the study. Ted Kaptchuk and colleagues worked with people who had irritable bowel syndrome. One group was given pills openly labeled placebo and told the truth: no active ingredient, but placebos can sometimes help. The other group got no pills, with the same warm attention from the staff. The placebo group reported more relief. Second, the honest size. It was a small study, of one condition, and the symptoms were reported by the patients themselves. So last week's question applies: was it repeated? A finding to hold with interest, not a cure. Third, what might be going on. The researchers point to the ritual around the pill: the bottle, the routine, the clear explanation, being taken seriously by someone who cares. The pill carried no medicine, but the ritual around it may have carried something. Fourth, the word itself. In the Latin Bible, a psalm line begins with that very word: "Placebo Domino in regione vivorum." The Douay-Rheims translation renders it: "I will please the Lord in the land of the living." Placebo: I will please. To be clear, none of this says anything about whether prayer or worship is real. Believers understand their own rituals in their own terms, and tomorrow takes up prayer directly. Today is smaller: a routine, done with care, seems to do something for the person doing it.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small ritual in your day, filling the kettle, lighting a candle, washing your face, the bell that starts this sit, and replay it slowly, step by step. Notice what your body does as it begins: does the breath change, do the shoulders drop? Don't decide what it means; just watch, and if you pray, notice what your own way of beginning prayer does too.
Honest placebo. Pills openly labeled as containing no medicine still helped some patients, perhaps through the ritual of care around them. Today's word.
Your line: ritual helps. The bottle was empty; the care around it wasn't. Tomorrow, prayer goes to the lab.

1332.title: Prayer in the lab
1332.hook: a careful study found no benefit from strangers praying for heart patients, and some believers say prayer isn't a lab tool (Benson et al.)
1332.howItsDone: People of faith pray in many ways, for themselves and for others; some say prayer is a relationship with God rather than something a study can measure, while skeptics point to trials that found no effect.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was honest placebo: pills openly labeled empty still helped some patients. Your line was ritual helps.

On a card: a first name and a last initial. That's all a small prayer group is handed. Somewhere else, a heart patient is waiting for bypass surgery, and the group has never met this person. They will pray for them anyway, as part of a study. Another group of patients gets no such prayers. A third group is told, for certain, that strangers are praying for them. Then the doctors count what happens after surgery, and people of faith and skeptics read the result very differently.
screen: `A NAME ON A CARD.` → `STRANGERS PRAY, AS PART OF A STUDY.` → `THEN THE DOCTORS COUNT.`

segments.voice: First, the study. A team led by the cardiologist Herbert Benson followed patients having heart bypass surgery at several hospitals. Some were prayed for by groups from religious communities who knew only a first name and a last initial. Some were not. And some were told plainly that they were being prayed for. Second, the result. Prayer from strangers made no measurable difference to complications after surgery. And the patients told for certain that they were being prayed for had somewhat more complications, not fewer. The study offers no settled explanation for that. Third, how some believers answered: they shrugged, and kept praying. Their point is older than any lab. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus is in the wilderness, dared to throw himself down from the temple so that angels will catch him. In the King James words, he answers: "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." To some readers, a controlled trial of God sounds a little like that dare: set up the test, then wait for heaven to perform. On this view, prayer is a relationship, not a dose of medicine. Fourth, how skeptics answered. If prayer from far away worked like a drug, a careful trial should catch it, and this one didn't. Both sides read the same paper. One says prayer isn't the kind of thing a lab can weigh. The other says the lab weighed it and found nothing. This path doesn't settle that argument. It asks you to hold both views with respect.

segments.voice: On an in-breath, bring up the first view: prayer is a relationship, and a lab can't weigh it. On the out-breath, the second: a careful test looked, and found nothing. Don't pick a winner; let both sit in the room the way two guests can share a couch, and if you pray, you can pray now as you usually do.
Prayer in the lab. A careful trial found no benefit from strangers' prayers for heart patients, and some believers answer that prayer was never a lab tool. Today's word.
Your line: not a lab tool. Both readings of that paper deserve a fair hearing. Until tomorrow.

1333.title: Community and health
1333.hook: attending services was linked to a lower risk of dying in a long study of nurses, and the cause is still debated (VanderWeele et al.)
1333.howItsDone: Religious communities gather weekly or more often for worship, and members often keep track of one another between services with visits, meals and calls.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prayer in the lab: one careful trial, two ways to read it. Your line was not a lab tool.

A folding chair. A paper cup of coffee gone lukewarm. Someone you only see on weekends asks how your mother's knee is doing, because they remembered from last time. Nothing about it is dramatic. It happens again next week, and the week after. Researchers wanted to know whether that kind of plain, repeated showing up does anything to a body over many years. They found a link. Then came the harder question, still argued about: is it the showing up that does it, or something hiding behind it?
screen: `A FOLDING CHAIR, A PAPER CUP.` → `SOMEONE REMEMBERS.` → `DOES SHOWING UP DO ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: First, the study. A team including Tyler VanderWeele looked at a long-running health study of nurses in the United States. The nurses reported how often they went to religious services, and the researchers followed their health in the years after. Second, the finding. Women who attended services more than once a week had a lower risk of dying during the study than women who never attended. Third, the honest part. Nobody assigned these nurses to go. Maybe people who are already healthier go more often. Maybe going helps. The researchers adjusted for health, habits and other differences, and the link held. But a study like this can't prove cause, and people still debate what might be doing the work: friends who notice when you're missing, a sense of meaning, fewer cigarettes, the steady rhythm of a week. Fourth, two old lines about the same habit. The Letter to the Hebrews, in the King James Bible, says: "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is." The reason it gives is encouragement, not a longer life: the next words are "but exhorting one another." Jewish tradition keeps a neighboring teaching in the Sayings of the Fathers, where Hillel says not to separate yourself from the community. Neither text promises good health. Both are about turning up for each other, week after week.

It doesn't need to be religious, and it doesn't need you to believe anything. See the door you'd walk through and one face on the other side, and let the breath carry that picture.

1334.title: Rituals calm us
1334.hook: a small, made-up ritual before a nerve-racking task lowered anxiety in lab studies (Brooks et al.)
1334.howItsDone: Religious life is full of small fixed rituals, like lighting candles, moving prayer beads or bowing before a meal; separately, performers and athletes often keep personal routines before a big moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was community and health: a long study linked showing up to a lower risk of dying. Your line was show up.

A basketball player at the free-throw line bounces the ball the same way every time, spins it once, breathes, and shoots. A grandmother taps the doorframe before a long drive. A student wears the same sweatshirt to every exam. Watch closely and you'll notice little routines like these right before a moment that matters. Are they just quirks? A team of researchers did something unusual to find out: they invented a ritual, handed it to strangers, and asked them to do something frightening.
screen: `THE SAME BOUNCE, EVERY TIME.` → `A TAP ON THE DOORFRAME.` → `AN INVENTED RITUAL, HANDED TO STRANGERS.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Alison Wood Brooks and her colleagues asked people to do nerve-racking things, like singing a pop song out loud in front of a stranger, or solving hard math problems under pressure. Second, the ritual. Before the task, some people were given steps: draw how you feel right now, sprinkle salt on the drawing, count to five out loud, crumple up the paper, throw it away. Others simply waited. Third, the result. The people who did the ritual reported less anxiety, had lower heart rates, and did better at the task. And the odd part: when the very same steps were described as random behaviors instead of a ritual, they helped less. The name mattered. Calling it a ritual seemed to tell the mind: this is the part where I get ready. Fourth, the honest edge. These were small lab studies, with a ritual invented on the spot. They say something about nerves before a task, and nothing about what a religious rite means to the people who keep it: candles lit on a Friday evening, beads moved one at a time, a bow before a meal. Those rites carry memory, community and faith, and a lab doesn't measure that. What the lab caught is one thin thread: a few fixed steps, done on purpose, can steady a person.

segments.voice: Think of one hard moment coming up, a meeting, a phone call, a conversation you've been putting off, and choose a few small steps for right before it: both palms flat on a table, one slow breath out, one word said silently, like ready, or here. Do the steps now, slowly, as a rehearsal. Then let your hands rest, and stay with the breath.
Rituals calm us. In lab studies, a few fixed steps before a frightening task lowered anxiety, especially when people called the steps a ritual. Today's word.
Your line: a tiny ritual. Your steps will be ready whenever the hard moment comes. Same time tomorrow.

1335.title: Singing together
1335.hook: in adult classes, people who sang together bonded faster than people in other classes (Pearce et al.)
1335.howItsDone: Congregations in several traditions sing together: hymns in churches, kirtan in Sikh gurdwaras, bhajans in Hindu temples, psalms and prayers sung in synagogues.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was rituals calm us: a few fixed steps, done on purpose, steadied nerves. Your line was a tiny ritual.

Nobody sings happy birthday well. The room starts in several keys at once, someone goes too high on the name, the candles drip wax on the frosting. And yet, by the last line, the room is together. People who were strangers when they walked in are laughing at the same off note. It would be easy to say that's just the cake. A team of researchers wondered whether singing itself does something to strangers, and how fast. Here's what they found, and the honest limits of it.
screen: `NOBODY SINGS HAPPY BIRTHDAY WELL.` → `BY THE LAST LINE, THE ROOM IS TOGETHER.` → `DOES SINGING DO IT?`

segments.voice: First, the classes. Eiluned Pearce, Jacques Launay and Robin Dunbar followed adult education classes, the kind people sign up for to learn something new. Some classes sang together. Others did crafts or creative writing. Second, the measure. At points through the course, people rated how close they felt to their classmates. Third, the finding: the singers bonded faster. Early on, people in the singing classes felt closer to each other than people in the other classes did, as if singing broke the ice. The authors called it an ice-breaker effect. Fourth, the honest part. Over the months, the other classes caught up. Crafts and writing made friends too; it just took longer. So singing isn't magic. It may be a shortcut to a place people reach in other ways. Traditions already sing together: hymns in churches, kirtan in Sikh gurdwaras, bhajans in Hindu temples, psalms sung in synagogues. One psalm opens with an invitation to sing as a group, in the King James words: "O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation." Notice the word us. And a joyful noise doesn't ask for good voices. It asks for voices together.

Singing together. In a study of adult classes, the people who sang together felt close faster than the others, who caught up later. Today's word.

1336.title: Fasting, honestly
1336.hook: the evidence on fasting for health is mixed; religious fasts are about meaning first
1336.howItsDone: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset during Ramadan, Jews fast on Yom Kippur, and Christians keep Lent in different ways; each tradition gives its fast a religious meaning and makes allowances, for example for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was singing together: the singers bonded faster, and the others caught up later. Your line was sing together.

A platter of sandwiches goes around a lunch meeting, and a coworker smiles and says, not today, thanks. A water bottle sits untouched on a desk on a hot afternoon. A family waits by the window for sunset before anyone reaches for a date. Across the world, people go without food for reasons that have nothing to do with a diet app. Meanwhile fasting has become a health trend, with plans and timers and big promises. Today holds both: what the research says, plainly, and what a religious fast is for.
screen: `NOT TODAY, THANKS.` → `WAITING FOR SUNSET.` → `A TREND, AND A PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: First, the trend. Fasting diets, skipping meals or eating only within certain hours, are sold as fixes for weight, energy and long life. Second, the evidence, plainly: it's mixed. Some readers of the research see benefits; others see little difference from simply eating less in an ordinary way. Some of the bigger promises run ahead of what has been shown. And fasting isn't safe for everyone: people who are pregnant, who have diabetes, or who have struggled with eating disorders are advised to talk with a doctor first. Third, what religious fasts are for. Here, meaning comes first. The Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, says: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." The aim it names is to ward off evil, not to lose weight, and the same passage excuses those who are sick or traveling, who make up the days later. The prophet Isaiah, in the King James Bible, asks what kind of fast God wants: "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free." There, a fast is measured by justice. Fourth, holding both. You can read the health studies with a skeptical eye and still honor the people nearby who fast for reasons no study measures: a Muslim neighbor in Ramadan, a Jewish friend on Yom Kippur, Christians keeping Lent in their own ways, seasons this path first met in its opening year.

segments.voice: Notice your own appetite right now, hungry, full or in between, without doing anything about it. Then bring to mind one person who keeps a fast, or one tradition's fast you've heard of, and what honoring it might look like: not eating in front of them, asking when they break the fast, learning the season's name. Fasting. The health research is mixed. Religious fasts put meaning first: warding off evil, and loosing the bands of wickedness. Today's word.
Your line: meaning first. A fast can be measured by more than a scale. Rest well.

1337.title: Slow breath, deeper
1337.hook: breathing at about six breaths a minute, with heart-rate biofeedback, has research support for stress and mood (Lehrer)
1337.howItsDone: Therapists who use heart rate variability biofeedback coach people to breathe slowly, often near six breaths a minute, while a screen shows their heart rhythm; similar slow breathing appears in yoga, Buddhist and Christian contemplative practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fasting, where religious fasts put meaning first. Your line was meaning first.

Your heart doesn't keep a perfectly even beat, and that's good news. Breathe in, and it speeds up a little. Breathe out, and it eases off. Two fingers on the inside of the wrist can sometimes catch it happening. This week has asked what holds up: an open placebo, prayer in a lab, showing up, a tiny ritual, singing together, fasting. It ends with something nobody has to believe in at all: that small rise and fall of the heart, and what happens when the breath slows down to meet it.
screen: `THE HEART SPEEDS UP, THEN EASES OFF.` → `A WEEK OF THE HONEST PART.` → `WHEN THE BREATH SLOWS TO MEET IT.`

segments.voice: First, the wave. That speeding up and easing off with each breath is normal. Researchers call the change from beat to beat heart rate variability. Second, the resonance. The psychologist Paul Lehrer and his colleagues worked with a simple idea. When people slow their breathing to around six breaths a minute, the heart's rise and fall lines up with the breath, and the waves grow larger, like pushing a child on a swing at just the right moment in each arc: small pushes, big swing. They called that pace the resonance frequency, and found it differs a little from person to person. Third, the evidence. With a screen showing their heart rhythm, people can learn to breathe right at that pace. This is heart rate variability biofeedback. Reviews of the studies have found it helps some people with stress, anxiety and low mood. It isn't a cure, and it isn't for everything, but it's one of the breath practices with real research behind it. Fourth, the old company. Breath has been a teacher on several paths: yoga's pranayama, Buddhist mindfulness of breathing, Orthodox Christians who join the Jesus Prayer to the breath. None of them needed a heart monitor. What the lab adds is a pace you can count, and a reason it might work. When breath and heartbeat move together, something in the body rings like a struck bell.
screen: `THE HEART'S RISE AND FALL.` · `BREATH AND HEART LINE UP.` · `BIOFEEDBACK: REAL SUPPORT, NOT A CURE.` · `AN OLD TEACHER, A NEW REASON.` · then, large: `AROUND SIX BREATHS A MINUTE.`

segments.voice: Breathe at about six a minute, roughly ten seconds for each whole breath: in gently through the nose for a slow count of four, out a little longer for a slow count of six. Don't force it or fill up hard, and if you feel lightheaded, let the breath go back to normal for a while. When the rhythm holds itself, let the count fade.
Slow breath. Around six breaths a minute, breath and heart rhythm line up, and biofeedback built on that has research support for stress and mood. Today's word.
Your line: resonant. In for four, out for six is there whenever stress rises. Breathe easy.
